title: Who Pays for the Smoke? Pricing Pollution and the Surprising Story of Where the Idea Came From
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: A History of Pricing Pollution (Or, Why Pigouvian Taxes are not Necessarily Pigouvian)

intro.summary: This lesson draws on four sources: two Wikipedia articles (on externalities and on Pigouvian taxes), an OpenStax textbook reading on pollution, and H. Spencer Banzhaf's 2020 NBER working paper on the history of pollution pricing. Together they teach the standard economics: when production harms bystanders, markets overproduce, and a charge equal to the harm (a 'Pigouvian tax') or a cap on tradable permits can fix that. They also cover alternatives such as private bargaining (Coase) and the problem of unowned 'commons'. Banzhaf asks where 1960s pollution-pricing proposals actually came from. He examines who cited whom and how the arguments were built, and finds that the pioneers barely mentioned Pigou. Their roots lay in American traditions of land, water and common-property economics, and the 'Pigouvian' label was applied around 1970. Limits: Banzhaf's paper is an unrefereed working paper whose evidence is partly citation counts and interpretive reading. The externality Wikipedia article carries warnings about possible AI-generated and one-sided content. Economists still disagree about whether such taxes can be measured and set correctly. Deeper follow-ups not covered here include positive externalities and subsidies, the 'double dividend' debate over recycling tax revenue, the measurement critique (Baumol, Buchanan), and ecological economists' rejection of the externality framing.
background: Economists picture a market as a demand curve (what buyers will pay for each extra unit) meeting a supply curve (what it costs sellers to make each extra unit).
'Marginal' means 'for one more unit': marginal cost is the cost of producing the next item.

Arthur Pigou was a Cambridge economist whose 1920 book The Economics of Welfare discussed gaps between private and social costs; Ronald Coase was a later economist known for arguing that people can sometimes bargain their way out of such problems.
A 'working paper' is circulated for comment before peer review, so its claims are still open to scholarly challenge.
intro.aha: The famous 'Pigouvian' pollution tax was mostly not built from Pigou's ideas: its 1960s inventors barely cited him, and the name was attached years later to work that grew out of American thinking about farmland, rivers and unowned commons.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: A factory that dumps waste into a river does not pay for the damage downstream, so its prices are too low and it makes too much. Economists call this kind of spillover an externality. The textbook answer is to charge the polluter for the harm, a remedy named after Arthur Pigou. Historian-economist H. Spencer Banzhaf asked a simple question: did the people who first designed pollution charges in the 1960s really get the idea from Pigou?
primer.quote: In economics, an externality is a cost or benefit to an uninvolved third party that arises as an effect of another party's (or parties') activity.

primer.heading: The standard tool
primer.body: In the textbook story, the harm adds an extra cost on top of what the firm pays. If the firm had to pay that extra cost per unit, prices would rise and output and pollution would fall to the level where benefits match full costs. The OpenStax reading works through a refrigerator example with a $100 per-unit pollution cost: the market moves from 45,000 to 40,000 refrigerators. Alternatives include capping pollution with tradable permits, or letting affected parties bargain.
primer.quote: If firms were required to pay the social costs of pollution, they would create less pollution but produce less of the product and charge a higher price.
primer.quote_where: OpenStax reading, 'Pollution as a Negative Externality'

primer.heading: What Banzhaf did
primer.body: Banzhaf reread the founding 1960s works on pollution pricing: Allen Kneese's 'effluent charges' and the tradable pollution rights of Thomas Crocker and John Dales. He traced whom they cited and how they argued, and he counted how often the phrase 'Pigouvian tax' appeared over time. He then compared those arguments with older American work on farmland, water rights, fisheries and resource development.

primer.heading: What he found
primer.body: The pioneers hardly cited Pigou at all. The phrase 'Pigouvian tax' appeared only about a dozen times in JSTOR in the 1960s, and it spread after Baumol and Oates called Kneese's work part of a 'Pigouvian tradition' around 1971. The arguments themselves came from American thinking about common property ('everybody's property is nobody's property') and the gains from developing rivers and land. The label came later and was attached to work already done.
primer.quote: This paper offers a simple explanation for this puzzle: Namely, pollution pricing is not (necessarily) Pigouvian.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: How we tell a tool's history shapes how we see it. Pollution pricing then looks less like a tax correcting a rare market glitch and more like a way to manage shared resources such as rivers and air. Banzhaf's case rests partly on citation counts and partly on interpretation, and the paper had not been peer reviewed. Economists also still debate the tool itself: whether harm can be measured well enough to set the right charge, and whether bargaining or regulation sometimes works better.
primer.quote: This paper has argued that the early literature on pollution pricing was rooted in questions about common property resources and the increasing returns from developing natural resources.

concepts.title: The hidden cost: private cost versus social cost
concepts.idea: When making a product harms bystanders, the true cost to society of each unit is the producer's own cost plus that external harm, so the full-cost supply curve sits above the one the market sees.

predict.question: A paper mill's own cost to make one more tonne of paper is $400. Its wastewater forces a downstream town to spend $60 per tonne cleaning its drinking water. It also kills fish worth $40 per tonne to local fishers. Where does the full-cost line sit for that tonne?
why: Tempting, because $400 is all the mill pays. That is the lower line the market sees. The full cost adds what others pay.
This counts the town's cleaning bill but forgets the fishers. Every bystander's harm goes into the gap, not just the most visible one.
Correct: own cost $400 plus $60 for the town plus $40 for the fishers. The full-cost line sits $100 above the mill's own line at this tonne.
This is only the gap, the harm to others. The full cost per tonne includes the mill's own $400 as well.

terms.means: What the producer itself pays to make one more unit
Harm from one more unit that falls on people outside the sale, who are not paid for it
The full cost of one more unit to everyone: the producer's own cost plus the external cost
A cost an activity imposes on uninvolved third parties that the market price leaves out

model.title: Two cost lines for making fridges
model.note: Teaching model: straight cost lines and the same harm for every fridge. The lines are built from the refrigerator example in source s3: the factory's line passes $600 at 40,000 fridges and $650 at 45,000, and the harm is $100 per fridge. In reality the harm can change with output, and putting a dollar value on it is hard. Harm values other than $100 are illustrative.

steps.say: This picture is about making fridges. Left to right is how many get made. Up is what one more fridge costs.
The lower line is what the factory itself pays for one more fridge: labour, metal, energy. It climbs as output grows.
The upper line adds the damage the factory's pollution does to people nearby: their health, their property, local wildlife.
This slider sets that damage for each fridge. Watch the upper line lift.
This slider picks one fridge to inspect. The boxes show what it costs the factory and what it costs everyone.

explore.prompt: Play with the harm and the fridge you inspect. Watch how far the full-cost line floats above the factory's line.

goals.text: Make the factory pay less than 80% of the true cost of the fridge you're inspecting.
hints: The share box compares the factory's own cost with the full cost. What would make the unpaid part bigger?
Raising the harm widens the gap. Inspecting a cheaper fridge also works, because the same harm is then a bigger slice of the total.
If you keep the inspected fridge where it starts, the harm has to go well above $150.

goals.text: Recreate a case where the factory's own cost for a fridge is $600 but its full cost to everyone is $800.
hints: You need to match two things: which fridge you inspect, and how big the harm is.
First slide the inspected fridge until the factory's own cost box reads 600.
Then set the harm to make up the difference between the two costs you want.

feedback.correct: Right. The full cost of a unit is the producer's own cost plus every bystander's harm from that unit: $400 + $60 + $40 = $500. The full-cost line sits above the private one by the whole external cost.
feedback.incorrect: The full-cost line is not the price the producer pays, and it is not the harm alone. It is the producer's own cost plus all the harm that falls on others. Add every bystander's loss to the mill's $400.

steps.say: Start with no harm at all. The two lines sit on top of each other: what the factory pays is the whole cost.
Now say each fridge's pollution does $100 of damage to people nearby. That is the figure in the textbook example. The upper line jumps up by exactly $100.
Economists name these lines. The lower one is the marginal private cost: what the maker pays for one more fridge. The upper one is the marginal social cost: that cost plus the harm to everyone else.
The vertical gap between them is the external cost. People outside the sale pay it, and nobody pays them back. A cost like that is called a negative externality.
Slide along the output. In this model the gap stays $100 everywhere, because every fridge adds the same harm.
Still $100 at 70,000 fridges.
At 40,000 fridges the factory's own cost is $600, but the cost to society is $700. Those are the textbook's numbers.
Make the harm bigger and the gap grows with it. At $250 of harm per fridge, the factory pays only about 71% of what this fridge really costs.

understand.explanation: Some costs of making a product fall on people who never bought or sold it, such as neighbours breathing a factory's smoke. So each extra unit has two costs: what the producer pays, and the producer's cost plus the harm to bystanders. On a chart this gives two supply lines, and the external cost is the vertical gap between them. The OpenStax textbook shows this with refrigerators. If pollution does $100 of damage per fridge and the firm had to pay it, its whole supply curve would shift up by $100: a firm that needed $600 to make 40,000 fridges would need $700. This model keeps the harm fixed per unit for clarity. Real harms can vary with output, and critics such as Baumol stress that putting a dollar figure on them is very hard.
understand.quote: The marginal private cost is less than the marginal social or public cost by the amount of the external cost, i.e., the cost of air pollution and water pollution. This is represented by the vertical distance between the two supply curves.
understand.quote_where: Externality (Wikipedia), section 'Supply and demand diagram', subsection 'External costs'

connect.caption: This is the standard accounting the sources describe in words, not an equation printed in them. The full cost to society of one more unit (MSC, marginal social cost, in blue-green) equals the producer's own cost (MPC, marginal private cost) plus the marginal external cost (MEC), which is the harm slider. In the model, MPC = 200 + 10 × (thousands of fridges), fitted to the OpenStax refrigerator table. MEC is constant, so the two lines stay parallel.

concepts.recap: Each unit's true cost is the producer's own cost plus the harm it does to others. That harm is the vertical gap lifting the full-cost supply line above the one the market sees.

concepts.title: Why the market makes too much
concepts.idea: Because buyers and sellers respond only to private cost, the market settles where demand meets private supply, which produces more than the quantity where benefit equals full social cost.

predict.question: A new filter makes the fridge factory's waste completely harmless, so the harm to bystanders per fridge drops to zero. What happens to the gap between what the market makes and the amount where buyer value equals full cost?
options: The gap disappears: the market now makes exactly the right amount
The market makes fewer fridges than before
The market still overshoots by 5,000 fridges
The market now makes too few fridges
why: Correct. With no harm, the full-cost line sits on top of the factory's line, so the two crossings with the buyers' line are the same point. The overshoot came only from the unseen harm.

It is tempting to think a cleaner factory changes output, but the factory's own costs did not move. The market's point stays at 45,000. Only the efficient point moves, and it moves up to meet the market's point.
The market's point does stay at 45,000. But the efficient point no longer sits 5,000 fridges below it. The gap was caused by the harm, and that harm is now zero.
The market would make too little only if buyers or makers were ignoring a benefit to others. Here nothing is left unpriced, so the market neither overshoots nor undershoots.

terms.means: The line showing the most buyers would pay for one more unit at each quantity
Where the demand curve meets the producer's own cost line: the price and amount a free market settles on
The amount where what buyers will pay for one more unit equals its full cost to everyone, harm included
When a free market's outcome leaves society worse off than another achievable outcome, for example because some costs go unpriced

model.note: Teaching model: straight lines and the same harm for every fridge. The buyers' line and the factory's cost line are built from the refrigerator table in source s3. Buyers take 50,000 fridges at $600, 45,000 at $650 and 40,000 at $700. The market settles at $650 and 45,000. With $100 of harm per fridge counted, it settles at $700 and 40,000. Harm values other than $100 are illustrative. The model assumes bystanders get no benefits from the fridges. Real harms can change with output and are hard to put in dollars.

steps.say: Same picture as before: the factory's own cost line, and the full-cost line sitting $100 above it because of the harm to bystanders.
New: this falling dashed line shows the most a buyer would pay for one more fridge. The first fridges go to keen buyers. Later ones go to buyers who care less, so the line slopes down.
Two dots mark where the buyers' line crosses each cost line. The harm slider still lifts the full-cost line. Watch which dot it moves.

explore.prompt: Play with the harm and the fridge you inspect. Watch which dot moves, which stays put, and when a fridge costs everyone more than it is worth to its buyer.

goals.text: Make the market overshoot the efficient quantity by exactly 6,000 fridges.
hints: Only one slider changes the size of the overshoot. Which line does it shift?
The market's dot never moves, so the efficient dot has to slide. Watch the 'Extra fridges made' box as you change the harm.
You need a bit more harm than the reading's $100, but well under $200.

goals.text: Find a fridge the market still makes whose full cost beats the most a buyer would pay by more than $150.
hints: Only fridges up to the market's dot get made. Of those, which one has the biggest loss?
Inspect the last fridge the market makes. Its loss is the full cost minus the buyer's top price, and each extra dollar of harm adds a dollar to it.
Keep the inspector on the market's dot, then raise the harm a little past the halfway mark of its slider.

feedback.correct: Right. The overshoot exists only because harm is left out of the price. With zero harm the full-cost line falls onto the factory's line, so the market's crossing is also the efficient one.
feedback.incorrect: The market's point never depended on the harm, because buyers and the factory never saw it. The harm only set where the efficient point sat. Remove the harm and that point rises to meet the market's point, so the gap closes.

steps.say: Start with no harm at all. The two cost lines lie on top of each other. The buyers' line, called the demand curve, crosses them at one spot: 45,000 fridges at $650.

Now add the reading's $100 of harm per fridge. The full-cost line lifts. Buyers and the factory still trade on the factory's own cost, so the market still settles at 45,000 fridges and $650. That spot is the market equilibrium.
The demand curve meets the full-cost line earlier, at 40,000 fridges and $700. This is the efficient quantity. Up to here, every fridge is worth at least its full cost to the person who buys it.
Inspect a fridge before that point, number 35,000. A buyer would pay up to $750, and its full cost is $650. Making it leaves everyone better off.

Now inspect the 45,000th fridge, the last one the market makes. A buyer would pay $650, but its full cost is $750. Society loses $100 on it, yet it is still made, because the bystanders who bear that $100 have no say in the deal.
Double the harm to $200. The market's dot does not budge. The efficient dot slides back to 35,000, so the overshoot doubles to 10,000 fridges.
At $300 of harm the market makes 15,000 fridges too many. Nobody is cheating: the price just never carries the harm. Economists call this a market failure.

understand.explanation: Buyers and the factory weigh only the factory's own cost, so trading stops where the demand curve crosses that line: the market equilibrium. The efficient quantity lies further left, where what a buyer will pay for one more fridge equals its full cost, harm included. Every fridge between the two points costs society more than it is worth to its buyer. Each one is still made, because the people deciding do not pay the difference. The textbook reading (s3) shows this with its refrigerator table: $650 and 45,000 fridges when pollution is free, and $700 and 40,000 once the $100 harm counts. The encyclopedia's steel example (s1) makes the same argument. In this straight-line model the overshoot grows in step with the harm. Real harms are hard to value, and the picture assumes no benefits to bystanders.
understand.quote: In the case of pollution, at the market output, social costs of production exceed social benefits to consumers, and the market produces too much of the product.
understand.quote_where: Pollution as a Negative Externality (OpenStax reading)

connect.caption: This is the model's own rule. The sources give the condition behind it: efficiency is where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost. MEC (orange, the harm slider) is the harm per fridge. 10 + 10 is how steep the buyers' line and the factory's line are, $10 per thousand fridges each. Harm divided by that total gives the overshoot in thousands of fridges (the 'Extra fridges made' box). It holds only for straight lines.

concepts.recap: The market settles where buyers meet the factory's own cost, so when harm goes unpriced it makes more than the amount where value equals full cost, and the overshoot grows with the harm.

concepts.title: A charge equal to the harm
concepts.idea: A per-unit charge equal to the marginal external cost lifts the private supply curve onto the social one, so the market itself picks the efficient quantity, which is lower but not zero.

predict.question: Regulators can't measure the harm well. The true harm is $100 per fridge, but they guess $250 and charge that much on every fridge. Compared with the efficient amount, what will the market do?
options: Make too few fridges: some fridges worth more to buyers than their full cost never get made
Make exactly the efficient amount, because a bigger charge is just the safe side
Still make too many fridges, because buyers simply pay the charge
why: Right. The charged line now sits above the full-cost line, so the market stops short. In this model it makes about 32,500 fridges instead of 40,000. The fridges in between were worth more to buyers than everything they cost society.

It is tempting to think that more caution can't hurt. The efficient amount is where buyer value equals full cost, though. A charge above the harm pushes the market past that point in the other direction.
A charge raises the cost of each fridge but doesn't forbid them. Buyers still value the first fridges far above even $250 plus the factory's cost, so production falls but goes on.

Buyers do pay part of the charge through a higher price, and that is exactly why they buy fewer. A charge larger than the harm cuts production below the efficient amount. It doesn't leave it too high.

terms.means: The harm one more unit of a product does to bystanders: here, the harm per extra fridge
A charge per unit set equal to the marginal external cost, so the producer pays for the harm it causes
Making the decision-maker pay a cost that used to fall on others, so their own sums now include it

model.title: Charging the fridge factory for the harm
model.note: Teaching model: straight lines and the same harm for every fridge. The buyers' line and the factory's cost line are built from the refrigerator table in source s3. With no charge the market settles at $650 and 45,000 fridges. With $100 of harm charged per fridge it settles at $700 and 40,000, which matches s3. Other harm and charge values are illustrative. The charge here is levied per fridge. Source s2 notes that a charge on the emissions themselves could also reward cleaner processes, which this model can't show, because each fridge's harm is fixed. The model assumes bystanders get no benefit from the fridges. It also assumes the regulator knows the harm, which real regulators rarely do.

steps.say: Same fridge market as before. Here is the buyers' line, the factory's own cost line, and the full-cost line that adds $100 of harm to bystanders per fridge.
New: this slider makes the factory pay a charge on every fridge it makes. The new line shows its own cost plus that charge.
The market now settles where buyers meet that charged line. Watch the market's marker slide left as the charge grows.

explore.prompt: You are the regulator now. Make the harm bigger or smaller, then try to tune the charge so the market itself lands exactly where buyer value meets full cost. Then see what happens when you overshoot.

goals.text: Make each fridge do more harm than it does at the start, then pick a charge that makes the market produce exactly the efficient amount.
hints: Which line has to land on top of which other line?
The charged line must sit exactly on the full-cost line, so the charge has to fill the whole gap between the factory's line and the full-cost line.
That gap is set by the harm slider. Compare the charge with the harm until the two markers meet.

goals.text: Keep the harm where it started and pick a charge that leaves the market 2,500 fridges short of the efficient amount.
hints: Falling short means the market's marker sits to the left of the efficient marker. What kind of charge does that?
Start from the charge that hits the efficient point exactly, then raise it further.
Each extra $20 of charge moves the market's amount left by 1,000 fridges. Work out how much more you need.

feedback.correct: Yes. The right charge equals the true harm. A charge built on a guess of $250 lifts the charged line above the full-cost line, so the market stops at about 32,500 fridges. The fridges between there and 40,000 were each worth more to buyers than their full cost, and society loses them. A badly measured charge misses in either direction.
feedback.incorrect: The goal is not as little production as possible. It is the amount where buyer value equals full cost. A charge bigger than the harm overshoots that point, so the market makes too few fridges, though it doesn't make zero. This is why critics in source s2 stress that the harm is hard to measure.

steps.say: Start with no charge and $100 of harm per fridge. The market makes 45,000 fridges, but buyer value equals full cost at 40,000: 5,000 too many.
Charge the factory $50 per fridge. Its cost line rises by $50, and buyers meet it at 42,500 fridges. That is closer, but still too many.

Now charge $100, exactly the harm each extra fridge does. The charged line lands right on the full-cost line, and the market settles at 40,000 fridges and $700. That matches the textbook table in source s3.

Economists call the harm from one more unit the marginal external cost. A charge equal to it is a Pigouvian tax. Nobody told the market 40,000. Buyers and the factory found that amount on their own once the factory paid for the harm.
Notice it is not zero. Forty thousand fridges are still made, because buyers value each of them at least as much as its full cost. The aim is the right amount of production, not none.
Overshoot to $200. The market drops to 35,000, now 5,000 short. Those lost fridges were worth more to buyers than everything they cost society.

So the right charge isn't a fixed number: it follows the harm. Raise the harm to $200 too, and the lines match again. This is called internalizing a cost: the factory now pays the harm it used to push onto bystanders.

understand.explanation: The market overproduced because the factory's sums left out the harm to bystanders. Charging the factory that harm on every unit lifts its cost line by exactly the gap, onto the full-cost line. Economists call this internalizing a cost. Buyers and sellers then settle by themselves at the efficient amount. Production is lower, but not zero, because buyers still value those fridges at least as much as their full cost. A charge below the harm still leaves too much, and one above it leaves too little. The textbook in source s3 shows this with refrigerators: a $100 charge per fridge moves the market from $650 and 45,000 to $700 and 40,000. Source s2 states the general rule and its main weakness. The charge must equal the true harm per unit, and Pigou himself, along with Baumol and others, warned that this harm is very hard to measure.
understand.quote: A tax shifts the marginal private cost curve up by the amount of the externality. If the tax is placed on the quantity of emissions from the factory, the producers have an incentive to reduce output to the socially optimum level.
understand.quote_where: Pigouvian tax, section 'Working of the Pigouvian tax'

check.task: Suppose each fridge does so much harm that fewer than 35,000 fridges are worth making. Set the harm to fit that, then choose the charge that gets the market to the right amount: not too many, not too few.
check.hint: First raise the harm until the efficient marker sits left of 35. Then tune the charge until the market's marker sits exactly on it, without going past it.
check.misconception: That a bigger charge is always better, or that the aim is to stop production. The right charge equals the harm per unit: anything larger pushes output below the efficient amount.

connect.caption: The model's rule in standard notation, not an equation printed in the sources. MPC is the factory's own cost line. The charge t (the new slider) lifts it. MSC, the full-cost line, is MPC plus MEC, the harm per fridge (the harm slider). The market hits the efficient amount only when t = MEC. Source s2 says it in words: 'Ideally, the tax is set equal to the external marginal cost.'

concepts.recap: Charge the producer exactly the harm each extra unit does, and the market itself stops at the efficient amount: fewer units, not none. Charging too little or too much misses.

concepts.title: Set the price or set the quantity
concepts.idea: Instead of setting a charge and letting quantity adjust, a regulator can cap total pollution with tradable permits and let the permit price adjust; aiming at the same target gives the same price.

predict.question: A town limits fridge pollution with tradable permits, set at the efficient amount. Then a new process cuts the factory's own cost of every fridge by $50, while the harm per fridge stays the same. With the permit limit unchanged, what happens?
options: The number of fridges stays at the limit, and the permit price rises by about $50
The factory makes more fridges, and the permit price stays the same
Both the number of fridges and the permit price rise
The permit price falls, because making fridges got cheaper
why: Right. The limit fixes the quantity, so only the price can move. At the limit, buyers still pay the same top price, but the factory's own cost is $50 lower. The gap a permit fills is therefore $50 wider.

That is what a fixed charge would do: with the price of polluting fixed, cheaper production means more fridges. Under a permit limit, nobody can make a fridge without a permit, so the quantity cannot grow.
Rising output would need more permits, and the limit doesn't change. All of the adjustment goes into the price.
Cheaper production makes each permit more valuable, not less. A permit is worth the buyer's top price minus the factory's cost at the limit, and that cost just fell.

terms.means: Fixing the total amount of pollution allowed by issuing permits, then letting firms buy and sell those permits
A fee per unit of pollution released; the 1960s name for what is now often called a Pigouvian tax
Price and quantity are two sides of one choice: fix either one and the market sets the other

model.title: Limit the permits or charge the factory
model.note: Teaching model: straight lines and the same harm for every fridge. Each permit covers the pollution from one fridge, so limiting pollution means limiting fridges. The buyers' line and the factory's cost line are built from the refrigerator table in source s3. With no charge the market settles at $650 and 45,000 fridges. With $100 charged per fridge it settles at $700 and 40,000. Permit counts, permit prices and other harm values are illustrative and come from no source. The model assumes everyone knows costs and demand exactly, which is why a charge and a limit aimed at the same target give identical results. Under real uncertainty they differ: source s1 notes that cap-and-trade reduces uncertainty about the final pollution level, and Dales argued that a charge needs trial and error to find the right price (s4). The model does not show who receives the permit money (permits sold or handed out free; see s2). It also does not show trading among firms with different clean-up costs. It assumes bystanders get no benefit from the fridges and that the regulator knows the harm.

steps.say: It's the same fridge market as before. The dashed line is what buyers would pay. The solid lines are the factory's own cost and the full cost including the harm to bystanders.

Here's the new slider. Instead of charging a fee, the town can hand out a limited number of pollution permits. Each one covers the pollution from one fridge, so no permit means no fridge. The new marker shows where the permits run out.
Permits can be bought and sold. This box shows what one trades for. While permits are plentiful, nobody pays anything for them.

explore.prompt: You're the regulator. First hit the best amount using permits alone. Then hit a different amount using the charge alone.

goals.text: With no charge on the factory, issue just enough permits that the market makes the amount where buyer value equals full cost.
hints: The charge stays at zero. Only the number of permits should do the work.
Find the green marker where buyer value equals full cost, and slide the permit limit onto it.
When you're there, the permit price should come out equal to the harm per fridge.

goals.text: Using the charge alone, get the market to make 37,500 fridges, while permits stay so plentiful they trade for nothing.
hints: A charge works like a permit price that the regulator sets directly.
Use the permit slider as a scout. Limit the permits to 37,500 and read the price they trade at.
Then raise the permit limit back up so permits are worthless again, and set the charge to the price you read.

feedback.correct: Yes. A permit limit pins the quantity, so any change in costs or demand shows up in the permit price. A fixed charge would do the opposite: the price of polluting stays put and the quantity moves.
feedback.incorrect: You may have reasoned as if the price of polluting were fixed, which is how a charge works. With a permit limit, the number of fridges can't change, so the adjustment must come through the permit price. That price is the buyer's top price minus the factory's cost at the limit.

steps.say: Let the harm be $200 a fridge. With no charge and permits to spare, the market makes 45,000 fridges. But buyer value only equals full cost at 35,000.
Issue permits for 60,000 fridges. Nothing happens. The market only wants 45,000, so permits aren't scarce and trade at $0.
Now issue permits for only 40,000. The factory would like to make more than that, so producers bid for the scarce permits. The price climbs until nobody wants more than 40,000.
The permit price is the gap at the limit. A buyer would pay $700 for fridge number 40,000, and the factory's own cost is $600. Holding a permit is worth that $100 difference.
This is cap-and-trade: fix the total and let trading set the price. Limit the permits to 35,000, where value equals full cost, and the permit price lands at $200. That is exactly the harm per fridge.
Now flip it. Remove the limit and charge $200 a fridge instead. In the 1960s this was called an effluent charge. The market makes 35,000 again, and permits fall back to $0.

Two routes reach one point. A $200 charge gives 35,000 fridges, and 35,000 permits give a $200 price. This is duality: choose the price and the quantity follows, or choose the quantity and the price follows.

understand.explanation: A charge fixes the price of polluting and lets the market choose how much gets made. A permit limit fixes how much gets made and lets trading choose the price. When permits are scarce, producers bid until a permit costs the gap between what buyers would pay and the factory's own cost at the limit. So a limit set at the efficient amount yields a permit price equal to the harm, the same number a correct charge would use. Banzhaf (s4) traces how Kneese proposed effluent charges in 1964, Crocker (1966) and Dales (1968) then proposed tradable pollution rights, and later work highlighted the duality between Kneese's prices and their quotas. The match is exact only when costs are known, as in this model. Under uncertainty, a charge leaves the amount of pollution uncertain and a limit leaves its price uncertain, which is one reason Dales preferred permits for their certainty over environmental quality.
understand.quote: Whereas effluent charges or pollution taxes set a price on pollution, allowing the market to determine the quantity demanded at that price, tradable permits set an upper bound on the quantity of pollution, allowing the market to determine the price at that quantity supplied.
understand.quote_where: Section 4 (Pollution Permits: Thomas Crocker and John Dales)

connect.caption: This is the model's rule; Banzhaf's history gives no equation. Q is the number of fridges made (thousands). It is whichever is smaller: the amount the market wants given the charge t, or the permit limit Q̄. The permit price p is the buyer's top price at Q minus the factory's cost plus charge at Q. When the limit doesn't bind, p is 0. When it binds, p plus t equals the gap, so a charge of p alone would produce the same Q.

concepts.recap: A charge fixes the price and lets the amount adjust; a permit limit fixes the amount and lets the price adjust. Aimed at the same target, they meet at the same point.

concepts.title: Could the neighbours just make a deal?
concepts.idea: If rights are clear and bargaining is cheap, the polluter and the harmed party can trade their way to an efficient outcome without a tax, but when many people are harmed, bargaining costs make this fail.

terms.means: Who the law says holds the right in a dispute, such as the right to let cattle roam or the right to undamaged crops
The costs of striking a deal: finding the other side, negotiating, and checking and enforcing the agreement
The claim that with clear rights and cheap bargaining, the parties reach the efficient outcome, whichever side holds the right
Someone who enjoys a benefit without paying their share, hoping others will pay

concepts.recap: Clear rights and cheap bargaining let two parties fix a spillover themselves; the rights only decide who pays. With many harmed people, bargaining costs swamp the gains and the deal fails.

understand.explanation: The earlier concept showed that a market overproduces because the producer ignores the harm to bystanders. The economist Ronald Coase asked whether the two sides could simply bargain the problem away without a tax: if the law makes clear who holds the right (the property rights), the side that cares more can pay the other, so the harm gets cut back whenever cutting it costs less than the damage. This idea, now called the Coase theorem, adds that the efficient result is the same whichever side holds the right. Only who pays whom changes. It needs strong conditions: clear rights, rational parties, complete information and low transaction costs, meaning the costs of finding each other, negotiating and enforcing a deal. When a factory's smoke harms thousands of people, those costs explode and each person is tempted to be a free rider who lets others pay. So bargaining usually fails there, and Spencer Banzhaf's 2020 history notes that Allen Kneese judged Coase's result unlikely to matter for water pollution for exactly this reason.
understand.quote: Economist Ronald Coase argued that individuals can come to an agreement with an efficient result without the need for a third party when transaction costs are low.
understand.quote_where: Pigouvian tax, 'Alternatives: No intervention (direct negotiation between parties)'

activities.title: The farmer and the rancher (made-up numbers)

steps.text: A rancher's cattle wander into a neighbouring farmer's field and trample crops worth $300 a year. The rancher could pen the cattle for $100 a year.
steps.result: Penning is the cheapest fix. It avoids $300 of damage for $100, a $200 gain.

steps.text: Rights version 1: the law gives the farmer the right to undamaged crops. The rancher must either pay $300 in damages or spend $100 on a pen.
steps.result: The rancher pens the cattle and pays $100.

steps.text: Rights version 2: the law gives the rancher the right to let cattle roam. The farmer would lose $300, so the farmer offers the rancher, say, $150 to pen them. The rancher gains $50 and the farmer saves $150.
steps.result: The cattle are penned and the farmer pays $150.

steps.text: Compare the two versions. In both the pen gets built, the efficient outcome. Moving the right only changed who pays.
steps.result: This is the Coase theorem: with clear rights and cheap bargaining, the outcome does not depend on who holds the right.

steps.text: Now add transaction costs. Suppose lawyers, meetings and checking that the pen stays shut cost $250 a year. In version 2 the whole gain from the deal is only $200.
steps.result: No deal is worth making. The cattle roam and $300 of crops are lost each year.

activities.takeaway: Bargaining fixes the spillover only when the gain from the deal is bigger than the cost of making it. Rights decide who pays, not whether the pen is built.

activities.title: Could bargaining work here?
activities.prompt: Each case comes from the sources. Sort it by whether private bargaining could plausibly reach an efficient deal without a tax or a rule.

cards.text: A rancher's cattle damage one farmer's crops.
cards.feedback: There are two parties, the harm is visible and the rights can be settled. One of them can pay the other to fence or pen the cattle. This is Coase's own example in the encyclopedia account.

cards.text: A logger who owns a forest plans to clear-cut it, which would hurt a nearby resort.
cards.feedback: The rights are clear and there are only two sides. The resort owner could pay the logger not to clear-cut, or buy the forest. The source calls this a case where the Coase theorem is relevant.

cards.text: Two neighbours disagree about a fence, noise or smoke.
cards.feedback: Coase argued it is cheaper for two neighbours to agree on these things than to bring in a third party. Transaction costs are low.

cards.text: A steel factory's smoke harms the lungs of a large number of people.
cards.feedback: No single person can practically negotiate with the plant, and organising thousands of people creates large transaction costs. The source says regulation is the more common approach.

cards.text: Vaccination protects everyone, so people would need to pay each other to get vaccinated.
cards.feedback: The whole population would have to self-organise to pay each other, and each person is tempted to free-ride. The source says such an organisation would be indistinguishable from government action.

cards.text: A logger wants to clear-cut a forest next to a resort, but the forest belongs to no one.
cards.feedback: Without well-defined, enforceable property rights there is nobody to strike a deal with and nothing to trade. The source calls this the most problematic situation from Coase's perspective.

activities.takeaway: Bargaining has a chance when few parties face each other over clear rights. It breaks down when the harmed are many or when no one owns the thing being harmed.
hints: Count how many people would have to sit at the table.
Then ask whether anyone clearly owns the right being traded.

activities.question: In the farmer-and-rancher example, a court moves the right from the farmer to the rancher. Bargaining is still cheap. What changes?

options.text: Who pays for the pen changes, but the cattle still get penned.
options.feedback: Correct. Penning saves $200 either way, so a deal happens either way. Only the payment flips, from the rancher paying to the farmer paying.

options.text: The cattle stop being penned, because the rancher no longer has to.
options.feedback: The rancher no longer has to, but the farmer will pay the rancher to pen them, since that is cheaper than losing $300 of crops. With cheap bargaining the efficient pen still gets built.
The outcome stays the same, but the money does not. Holding the right is worth something, so the side without it ends up paying.

options.text: The rancher must now pay the farmer even more.
options.feedback: It is the other way round. Once the rancher holds the right, the farmer is the one who pays.

hints: Look back at rights versions 1 and 2 in the worked example.

activities.question: One power plant's fumes reach 200,000 residents of a city. A friend says: 'No tax needed. The residents and the plant can just negotiate.' Which condition for a Coase-style deal fails most plainly?

options.text: Bargaining would be far too costly: 200,000 people would have to find each other, agree on terms, share the bill and enforce the deal.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the steel-plant case in the sources. Transaction costs swamp the gains, and many residents would free-ride, hoping others pay.

options.text: The plant's owners would behave irrationally.
options.feedback: Nothing in the case suggests this. The plant may act very sensibly. The obstacle is the cost of organising the other side.

options.text: There is no harm to bargain over.
options.feedback: The fumes do harm people, so there is something to trade. The problem is that trading it is impractical.

options.text: The efficient result would depend on whether the plant or the residents hold the right.
options.feedback: The Coase theorem says the opposite when its conditions hold: the efficient result is the same either way. Here the conditions do not hold, mainly because bargaining is so costly.

hints: Compare this case with the steel factory card you sorted.
Think about what it costs just to get everyone to the table.

concepts.title: Everybody's property is nobody's property
concepts.idea: When nobody owns a resource like a fishery or a river, users keep crowding in until its value is used up, so putting a price on access is a way to manage the shared resource.

predict.question: A river authority starts charging every boat a yearly fee to fish. The fee is set at a well-chosen level, and anyone who pays may still come in. What happens to the fishery?
options: Fewer boats join. The fleet settles nearer the best size, and much of the value once burned up on extra boats is now collected as fees
The fleet stays the same size and fishers simply earn less
Every boat leaves and the fishery shuts down
More boats join, because each one must catch more fish to cover the fee
why: Right: newcomers now stop joining when profit per boat minus the fee hits zero, which happens sooner. A well-set fee holds the fleet near the best size. The leftover value then shows up as fee revenue instead of being eaten by surplus boats.

Tempting if you picture the fee as a pure transfer of money. But entry is driven by profit per boat. Once the fee cuts that profit below zero at the old fleet size, some boats stop coming, so the fleet shrinks.

A fee that is far too high could do this. A well-chosen fee only removes the extra boats whose catch merely comes out of other boats' catch. The best fleet still earns enough to cover its costs and the fee.

This mixes up one boat's effort with the number of boats. In this model each boat's catch depends on how crowded the water is, not on how badly its owner needs money. A fee lowers profit per boat, so fewer boats join.

terms.means: A resource that anyone can use without asking permission or paying, because nobody owns or controls entry to it
The money a resource yields after paying all the costs of using it: here, the catch value minus the cost of the boats
A resource such as a fishery, a river or the air that is shared, so one user's use reduces what is left for others

model.title: A shared fishery: value of the catch as more boats join
model.note: Teaching model: a simple fishery in the style of Gordon (1954). Boats are identical and the fish price is fixed. The yearly catch value rises and then falls as boats crowd a shared fish stock, following value = 4N − 0.04N² in $ thousands, where N is the number of boats. It leaves out how fish numbers change over time, differences between boats and moving prices. All numbers are illustrative, not data from the paper or from Gordon.

controls.label: Yearly cost of running one boat

outputs.label: Profit per boat (what a newcomer can expect)
Fleet with the most money left over

steps.say: This curve is the yearly value of all the fish caught, for each number of boats. It rises at first, but crowded boats thin out the fish, so it peaks and then falls.
The straight line is what all the boats together cost to run.
This slider adds or removes boats. The line marked 'Your fleet' follows it.
This slider sets the yearly cost of one boat. Watch the cost line tilt.
Two markers matter: where new boats stop joining, and where the money left over is largest.

explore.prompt: Now you run the fishery. Move the boats and the cost per boat. Find where crowding stops and where the shared value peaks.

goals.text: Put the fleet exactly where newcomers stop joining, and arrange things so that this stopping point falls at the very top of the catch curve.
hints: Newcomers stop joining when profit per boat reaches zero. You need that to happen at the peak of the catch curve.
First park the fleet at the top of the catch curve. Then change the cost per boat until profit per boat is zero.
At the peak, the cost that stops entry equals the catch value there divided by the number of boats there.

goals.text: Make running a boat cheaper than it is now. Then find the fleet size that leaves the most money over after paying for the boats.
hints: Lower the cost first. The best fleet is not the place where newcomers stop joining.
Watch the 'Money left over' box as you add boats one at a time. Stop where it is highest: there, one more boat adds only as much catch value as it costs.
With this simple catch curve, the best fleet is half the size of the fleet where newcomers stop, at the same cost.

feedback.correct: Yes. A fee raises the bar for joining: boats now stop coming when profit per boat minus the fee reaches zero. Set near the right level, the fee holds the fleet close to the best size. The value that crowding used to burn up is collected as fee revenue instead. This is the logic behind treating access to rivers and air as something to price.
feedback.incorrect: The key is that the number of boats responds to profit per boat. Under free access, boats keep coming until that profit is zero. A fee lowers profit per boat at every fleet size, so entry stops sooner. A sensible fee shrinks the fleet toward the best size without emptying the fishery, and the leftover value goes to the fee collector instead of to surplus boats.

steps.say: Start with an empty fishery: no boats, no catch. A boat costs 1.6 thousand dollars a year to run.
Add 20 boats. Each one earns 1.6 thousand more than it costs, so word spreads and more boats want in.
Nobody owns this water, so nobody can turn a boat away. Economists call this open access. Boats keep arriving until profit per boat hits zero, here at 60 boats.
Look at the money left over: zero. The catch is worth 96 thousand and the boats cost 96 thousand. All the fishery's value has gone into running extra boats.
Pull back to 30 boats. The catch is a little smaller, 84, but costs fall much more, to 48, leaving 36 thousand over. This leftover is the resource rent, and 30 boats is where it peaks.

So why doesn't the crowd stop at 30? A newcomer there still expects 1.2 thousand profit, so it joins. Its catch partly comes out of everyone else's nets, a cost it doesn't pay. The fishery is a common property resource.
Now make boats cheaper. Entry runs even further, to 75 boats: past the peak, where more boats catch less fish in total. The money left over is zero again.

understand.explanation: When nobody owns a fishery, nobody can turn a boat away. Boats keep joining as long as one more boat expects to earn more than it costs. Each newcomer thins the fish for everyone else, a cost it does not pay. So entry runs past the fleet that leaves the most money over, and stops only when the leftover value, the resource rent, has been used up. Gordon (1954) and Scott (1955) showed this formally for fisheries. The paper argues that Kneese, Crocker and Dales reasoned from the same logic: rivers and air are shared resources treated as free, so a public price on using them, such as effluent charges or tradable rights, can close off free access. This is a teaching model: real fisheries have changing fish stocks, different boats and moving prices. A fee only helps if it is set near the right level, which is hard to know. Quotas, permits and community management are other ways to manage a commons.
understand.quote: Both recognized the wisdom in the popular aphorism that "everybody's property is nobody's property," but demonstrated formally how under open access competition would deplete the value of resources.
understand.quote_where: Section 5, 'Property Rights and Land Tenancy' (on Gordon 1954 and Scott 1955)

equation.text: Most left over when one more boat adds  ΔR =

connect.caption: This is the teaching model's rule, in the style of Gordon (1954); the paper itself prints no equation. R(N) is the value of the whole catch with N boats, and c is the yearly cost of one boat. Under free access, boats join until the average catch per boat just covers c. The best fleet is smaller: it stops where one more boat adds only c to the total catch. With this catch curve, the best fleet is half the free-access fleet.

concepts.recap: Under free access, users crowd in until the resource's surplus is gone; putting a price on access can hold use near the best level.

concepts.title: The tax that wasn't named for its source
concepts.idea: Evidence from citations and arguments shows that 1960s pollution pricing grew from American common-property and resource-development traditions, and the 'Pigouvian' label was attached around 1970.

terms.means: A fee for each unit of waste a firm releases into a river or the air. It was the 1960s name for what is now called a Pigouvian tax.
Something many people use but nobody owns, such as a fishery, a river or the air.
A research paper circulated for discussion before it has been peer-reviewed.

concepts.recap: 1960s pollution pricing grew from American thinking about commons, rivers and resource development; Pigou's name was attached around 1970. That is an argued case, not settled fact.

understand.explanation: The pollution charge from the earlier concepts is now called a 'Pigouvian tax', after Arthur Pigou, whose 1920 book described costs that fall on bystanders. In a 2020 working paper (circulated for comment, not peer-reviewed), the historian Spencer Banzhaf argues that the name hides the real family tree. In 1964 Allen Kneese proposed an effluent charge, a fee per unit of waste dumped into rivers, and in 1966–68 Thomas Crocker and John Dales proposed tradable pollution rights. None of them cited Pigou in that work: a Google Scholar search for 1962–72 found 982 works mentioning Kneese without Pigou and only 65 mentioning both. Instead they drew on Coase and on American resource economics, such as Scott Gordon's 1954 study of a fishery as a common-property resource that everyone uses and nobody owns, groundwater law, and the spillovers of dams and irrigation. The 'Pigouvian' label spread only around 1971, when Baumol and Oates placed Kneese in a 'Pigouvian tradition'. So the famous tax was mostly not built from Pigou: his name was attached later to work rooted in American thinking about farmland, rivers and unowned commons. This is an argued reading, not a settled consensus.
understand.quote: This paper has argued that the early literature on pollution pricing was rooted in questions about common property resources and the increasing returns from developing natural resources. Both topics were treated by broad literatures by the 1960s, including distinctly American traditions not particularly associated with Pigou.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened, from earliest to latest.
items: Pigou's The Economics of Welfare describes costs and benefits that fall on bystanders
Scott Gordon analyses the fishery as a resource everyone uses and nobody owns
Kneese proposes effluent charges on river pollution, without citing Pigou
Crocker and Dales propose tradable pollution rights, with no reference to Pigou
Baumol and Oates describe Kneese's work as part of a 'Pigouvian tradition'
Textbooks and literature reviews make the 'Pigouvian' label standard
activities.explanation: Pigou's book appeared in 1920, with a 4th edition in 1932. Gordon's common-property paper followed in 1954. Kneese's effluent charges came in 1964, and Crocker's and Dales's tradable rights in 1966 and 1968. Only in 1971 did Baumol and Oates place Kneese in a 'Pigouvian tradition', and textbooks such as Baumol and Oates (1975) then made it standard. The gap matters: the tools existed for years before anyone named them after Pigou, and Gordon's work on the commons sits right before them.
hints: Banzhaf's evidence is that the inventors came first and the name came after.
The two proposals by the 1960s pioneers come before anything that uses the word 'Pigouvian'.
Gordon's fishery paper was one of the few references Crocker and Dales gave, so it must come before them.

activities.question: Which passage best supports the claim that the 'Pigouvian' name was attached to pollution pricing later, rather than inherited from its origins?

options.quote: Though the moniker "Pigouvian" was adopted around 1970, the name should not be confused with hereditary lineage.
options.feedback: Yes. This passage dates the label to around 1970 and says directly that the name is not evidence of descent from Pigou. That is the core of Banzhaf's claim.

options.quote: Pigou's discussion seems like a natural source for economic thinking about environmental problems.
options.feedback: Banzhaf writes this, but only to set up the conventional story he then questions. On its own it says Pigou looks like a natural source, which is the opposite of what we need.

options.quote: Because of high transactions costs, Kneese thought that Coase's negotiation result was unlikely to be relevant to water pollution problems.
options.feedback: This passage is about Kneese's view of Coasean bargaining (the 'make a deal' idea from an earlier concept). It shows he engaged with Coase, but it says nothing about when the Pigouvian label appeared.

options.quote: Pigouvian taxes are named after the English economist Arthur Cecil Pigou (1877–1959), who developed the concept of economic externalities.
options.feedback: This passage, from the encyclopedia article, tells you whom the tax is named after. It does not say when the name arrived or whether the people who designed pollution charges actually drew on Pigou. It reflects the conventional story Banzhaf is challenging.

hints: Look for a passage that mentions a date for the name.
The right passage separates what something is called from where it came from.

activities.title: What the pioneers actually drew on
activities.prompt: For each item, decide whether it shows up as an influence in the 1960s pioneers' work or is missing from it, according to Banzhaf.

cards.text: Kneese: Coase's bargaining idea and his theory of the firm
cards.feedback: Present. Kneese introduced Coasean bargaining early in his 1964 book and used a 'basin-wide firm', drawn from Coase's 1937 paper, as an organising idea.

cards.text: Kneese: spillovers from water projects, like irrigation recharging neighbours' wells
cards.feedback: Present. Before turning to pollution, Kneese studied external economies of water development, which came from resource-development economics.

cards.text: Kneese: Pigou, when discussing effluent charges in the 1960s
cards.feedback: Missing. After a 1960 paper on welfare economics, Kneese did not cite or mention Pigou until the end of the decade.

cards.text: Dales: Scott Gordon's 1954 paper on the fishery as a common-property resource
cards.feedback: Present. Dales named Gordon among his intellectual debts, and Crocker later discussed Gordon's model of the commons too.

cards.text: Dales: Coase's 'The Problem of Social Cost'
cards.feedback: Present. Dales acknowledged 'owing much' to it, though Banzhaf says this was more for its general link between law and economics.

cards.text: Crocker: the old doctrine of absolute ownership of groundwater
cards.feedback: Present. Crocker had helped his advisor Mason Gaffney on western water law, and he compared rights to air with that groundwater doctrine.
Missing. Banzhaf finds 'absolutely no reference' to Pigou in either Crocker's or Dales's work.

activities.takeaway: The pioneers' references point to Coase and to American traditions on commons, water law and resource development, not to Pigou. That positive evidence is what lifts Banzhaf's case beyond a mere absence of citations.

activities.question: How much weight should you put on Banzhaf's conclusion?

options.text: A lot: the citation counts and the pioneers' own references point the same way.
options.feedback: There is real support for this. Several independent kinds of evidence line up: the JSTOR count (only 12 uses of 'Pigouvian tax' in the 1960s), the Google Scholar split, and the references to Gordon, Coase and water law. The limit is that citation searches are rough tools, and the argument rests on one author's reading of a limited set of texts, mostly American ones.

options.text: Some caution: missing citations might just mean Pigou's ideas were so standard that nobody bothered to cite them.
options.feedback: This is a fair worry, and Banzhaf raises it himself. He even notes Kneese's line that economists 'have long held' that spillovers can be taxed, which hints at an unwritten tradition. His reply is that the pioneers' arguments and actual references point to other sources. That narrows the worry, but it cannot fully rule out an unwritten influence.

options.text: Treat it as a well-argued case still awaiting scrutiny, because it is an unrefereed working paper.
options.feedback: This is supported by the paper itself, which states that NBER working papers 'have not been peer-reviewed'. Other historians, such as Medema, have raised related doubts about a Pigovian lineage, which adds some support. The encyclopedia articles still tell the conventional Pigou story, so this remains an open debate rather than a consensus.

options.text: It proves Pigou had no influence at all on pollution pricing.
options.feedback: This goes beyond what the paper says. Banzhaf calls the Pigouvian approach 'undeniably an important source' but 'one of many'. His claim is that the lineage was overstated and that whole traditions were overlooked. He does not claim Pigou was irrelevant, and he does not question the economics of the tax itself.
